title: Signal Over the South Bay: Field Guide
fiction: Companion to an original comic. Items tagged REAL are real South Bay species, places or phenomena; items tagged INVENTED belong to the comic's fictional world and are not real ecology.

items.name: Sea Fig
items.description: A trailing succulent of the ice plant family that mats over sand with fat, three-sided leaves. Its magenta flowers open in full sun and close when the marine layer rolls in.
items.fun_fact: Each leaf is a little canteen: the plant stores water inside so it can live on sand that drains in seconds.

items.name: Beach Evening Primrose
items.description: A low, silver-gray dune plant that spreads in a rosette across the sand. Its four-petaled yellow flowers brighten the foredunes from spring into fall.
items.fun_fact: The yellow blossoms blush reddish as they age, so one plant can wear two colors at once.

items.name: Beach Sand Verbena
items.description: A sprawling native with round clusters of pink-to-magenta flowers on long sandy runners. It is one of the first colors you see on a restored dune.
items.fun_fact: Its leaves are sticky, so they wear a coat of sand grains, a kind of beach camouflage and sunscreen.

items.name: Silver Beach Lupine
items.description: A rounded shrub of soft silver leaves and spikes of lavender-blue pea flowers. It anchors the back dunes and feeds the soil around it.
items.fun_fact: Fine silver hairs on its leaves bounce sunlight away, keeping the plant cool on a blazing dune.

items.name: Beach Bur
items.description: A gray-green, sprawling dune plant with deeply cut leaves. Its spiny little burs hitch rides on fur, feathers and beach towels.
items.fun_fact: It is a cousin of ragweed and one of the toughest pioneer plants on a moving dune.

items.name: Grunion Run
items.description: On spring and summer nights just after the highest tides, silver grunion surf onto the beach to spawn in the wet sand. The eggs incubate in the sand until the next big tides wash them out to hatch.
items.fun_fact: Grunion are among the only fish in the world that leave the water entirely to lay their eggs.

items.name: Pacific Mole Crab
items.description: The little sand crab that kids dig up in the swash zone, shaped like an egg with legs. It rides each wave up the beach and burrows backward in a flash.
items.fun_fact: It eats by holding up feathery antennae in the backwash to comb plankton from the water.

items.name: Beach Hopper
items.description: A pale, long-antennaed amphipod that hides under kelp by day and boings across the sand at night. It is the beach's cleanup crew.
items.fun_fact: Beach hoppers navigate by the moon and the slope of the beach to find their way back to the wrack line.

items.name: Wrack Line
items.description: The ribbon of washed-up kelp and seagrass that marks the last high tide. It is a buffet for flies and hoppers, and those feed the shorebirds.
items.fun_fact: Beach groomers that rake the wrack away also rake away the food that snowy plover chicks depend on.

items.name: Sea Glass
items.description: Bottle glass that has been tumbled by surf and sand until it turns frosted and smooth. Locals keep jars of it on windowsills all along the coast.
items.fun_fact: It can take 20 years or more of tumbling to frost a shard, and red and orange pieces are among the rarest finds.

items.name: Marine Layer
items.description: A low gray blanket of cloud that drifts in from the cold Pacific on spring and summer mornings. It usually burns off by midday and creeps back at dusk.
items.fun_fact: Locals call its seasons May Gray and June Gloom; it keeps the beach towns cooler than inland LA.

items.name: Signal Sand
items.description: In this world, a strip of quartz sand near the pier that faintly hums whenever the Lantern broadcasts. Beachgoers press an ear to the sand to hear the morning edition early.
items.fun_fact: Invented for the comic: the sand is said to go silent at 4:12 A.M., which is how the town knew something was wrong.

items.name: Jet-Wash Dune Grass
items.description: An invented dune grass whose seed heads lean toward the runways and fly off in the wake of every takeoff. It spreads along the coast one departure at a time.
items.fun_fact: Invented: field notes claim you can tell the last flight's direction by the way the grass is combed.

items.name: Giant Kelp
items.description: A golden-brown seaweed that rises from the rocky bottom to the surface in towering underwater forests. Gas-filled bulbs hold its blades up toward the light.
items.fun_fact: In good conditions it can grow up to about two feet in a single day.

items.name: Feather Boa Kelp
items.description: A long, strap-shaped brown kelp fringed with tiny blades that make it look like a feather boa. It drapes over rocks in the low intertidal.
items.fun_fact: Its frond can stretch longer than a city bus and still flex with every wave.

items.name: Eelgrass
items.description: A bright green, ribbon-leaved plant that forms underwater meadows in calm bays and harbors. Its beds shelter baby fish, crabs and scallops.
items.fun_fact: Eelgrass is not seaweed; it is a true flowering plant that blooms and pollinates underwater.

items.name: Surfgrass
items.description: A vivid emerald flowering plant that grows in shaggy mats on surf-swept rocks. At low tide it lies combed flat like wet hair.
items.fun_fact: Like eelgrass it is a true seagrass, holding on with roots in places that would rip most plants away.

items.name: Giant Green Anemone
items.description: A big, jade-green sea anemone that lines tide pools with a ring of sticky tentacles. It catches mussels, crabs and anything the waves knock loose.
items.fun_fact: Its green glow comes partly from tiny algae living inside its tissues and sharing the sunlight.

items.name: Ochre Sea Star
items.description: A sturdy, five-armed sea star in purple or orange that clings to rocks in the mid-tide zone. It pries open mussels with steady pull.
items.fun_fact: It is the original keystone species: scientists found that removing it lets mussels take over the whole shore.

items.name: Purple Sea Urchin
items.description: A spiny violet grazer that wedges itself into rock and munches drift kelp. When predators disappear, urchins can swarm and mow down a forest.
items.fun_fact: Bare rock left behind by too many urchins is called an urchin barren.

items.name: California Mussel Bed
items.description: Dense blue-black beds of mussels that coat the rocks where waves crash hardest. Hundreds of small creatures live in the spaces between shells.
items.fun_fact: Mussels anchor with silky byssal threads strong enough that engineers study them for underwater glues.

items.name: Owl Limpet
items.description: A large, flat limpet that tends a private patch of algae on the rocks. It bulldozes intruders off its turf.
items.fun_fact: Owl limpets start life male and can turn female as they grow larger.

items.name: Blue-Glow Tide
items.description: A bloom of plankton that tints the water reddish by day and makes breaking waves flash electric blue at night. It shows up some years along Southern California beaches.
items.fun_fact: The glow is bioluminescence: each tiny cell flashes when the water jostles it.

items.name: California Two-Spot Octopus
items.description: A small, shy octopus that hides in rocky crevices and tide pools. A blue eyespot ring sits below each eye.
items.fun_fact: It can change both color and skin texture in a fraction of a second to vanish against a rock.

items.name: Tide-Clock Barnacles
items.description: An invented acorn barnacle colony on the pier pilings that opens all at once at 6:45 every morning. Pier fishermen set their watches by them.
items.fun_fact: Invented: they stayed shut on the morning the Lantern went dark, and opened late, right when the signal returned.

items.name: Radio Abalone
items.description: An invented abalone whose rainbow shell lining catches stray broadcasts like a crystal radio. Divers hear faint music when they hold one to their ear.
items.fun_fact: Invented: real abalone are protected in California, so in this world the radio kind are only listened to, never taken.

items.name: El Segundo Blue Butterfly
items.description: A thumbnail-size butterfly found only in a few coastal dune remnants around El Segundo and the LAX dunes. Males are bright blue above; females are brown with an orange band.
items.fun_fact: It was among the first insects listed under the U.S. Endangered Species Act in 1976, and it lives almost its whole life on one plant.

items.name: Seacliff Buckwheat
items.description: A low native shrub with small leaves and flat clusters of cream-to-pink flowers. It is the El Segundo Blue's only host plant.
items.fun_fact: Restoration crews plant it by the thousands; more buckwheat means more butterflies the next summer.

items.name: El Segundo Blue Caterpillar
items.description: The tiny larva feeds on buckwheat flowers in summer and then drops into the sand below to pupate. It waits there, sometimes for more than a year, until the next bloom.
items.fun_fact: Its pink-and-cream coloring matches the buckwheat flower heads it eats.

items.name: LAX Dunes
items.description: The largest surviving stretch of the old El Segundo dune system, beside the airport's runways. Fenced and restored, it is home base for the butterfly.
items.fun_fact: Once, these dunes stretched for miles from Westchester to Palos Verdes; the preserve is a small saved piece.

items.name: Coastal Sagebrush
items.description: A soft, gray-green native shrub with threadlike leaves and a sharp herbal scent. It is a backbone plant of coastal sage scrub.
items.fun_fact: Old-timers called it cowboy cologne for the smell it leaves on your hands.

items.name: Deerweed
items.description: A wiry, green-stemmed native shrub dotted with small yellow pea flowers that age to red. It is often first to grow back after a disturbance.
items.fun_fact: Its roots host bacteria that pull nitrogen from the air, fertilizing the dune for everything else.

items.name: California Poppy
items.description: The state flower, with silky orange cups that light up open ground in spring. It pops up along the dune edges and roadsides.
items.fun_fact: Poppies fold their petals shut at night and on cloudy days, and open again in the sun.

items.name: Globose Dune Beetle
items.description: A small, round, dark beetle that lives in loose coastal sand. It is rare and depends on healthy native dunes.
items.fun_fact: It cannot fly; it swims through the sand just under the surface instead.

items.name: Mock Heather
items.description: A dense, needle-leaved native shrub that blooms in bursts of tiny yellow flowers in late summer and fall. Bees crowd it when little else is flowering.
items.fun_fact: Its late bloom is a lifeline for pollinators at the end of the dry season.

items.name: California Croton
items.description: A small, silvery dune plant with felted leaves and tiny greenish flowers. It holds loose sand in place.
items.fun_fact: Each plant is either male or female, so it takes two to make seed.

items.name: Blue-Hour Buckwheat
items.description: An invented buckwheat that opens only at dusk, when the Lantern's beacon first glows. The butterflies in this world take a second, evening flight to visit it.
items.fun_fact: Invented: the flowers are said to glow faintly teal, matching the beacon above.

items.name: Periwinkle Static
items.description: An invented shimmer of static charge that sparkles off El Segundo Blue wings on dry Santa Ana afternoons. It looks like blue glitter in the air above the preserve.
items.fun_fact: Invented: on the field guide's map it is the reason the preserve fence hums.

items.name: Pickleweed
items.description: A succulent marsh plant made of jointed green stems that look like strings of tiny pickles. It carpets the salt marsh in green that turns red in fall.
items.fun_fact: It soaks up salt into its stem tips, which turn red and drop off, taking the salt with them.

items.name: Pacific Cordgrass
items.description: A tall marsh grass that grows along the lowest, wettest edge of the salt marsh. Tides flood it twice a day.
items.fun_fact: It pushes extra salt out through its leaves, leaving glittering crystals on the blades.

items.name: Saltgrass
items.description: A low, tough grass that forms mats on the higher, drier parts of the marsh. It spreads by underground runners.
items.fun_fact: It literally sweats salt: tiny crystals sparkle on its leaves on sunny days.

items.name: Alkali Heath
items.description: A low, gray-green marsh shrub with tiny pink flowers. It edges salt pans where little else will grow.
items.fun_fact: It handles salty, waterlogged soil that would kill most garden plants.

items.name: Arroyo Willow
items.description: A shrubby willow that lines the freshwater marsh and creek edges. Songbirds nest in its thickets.
items.fun_fact: Willow bark contains salicin, the natural compound behind aspirin.

items.name: Striped Shore Crab
items.description: A square-bodied crab with green and purple stripes that scuttles over rocks and marsh banks. It eats algae and whatever it can scavenge.
items.fun_fact: It can stay out of water for long stretches and even climbs walls and pilings.

items.name: California Horn Snail
items.description: A small, tall-spired brown snail that crowds the mudflats by the thousands. It grazes the film of algae on the mud.
items.fun_fact: At low tide whole mudflats can be dotted with them like scattered rice.

items.name: Tidal Creek
items.description: A winding channel that fills and drains the marsh with every tide. Fish, crabs and birds follow the water in and out.
items.fun_fact: The creek's curves are made by the tide itself, carving new bends year after year.

items.name: Mudflat
items.description: Shining mud that appears when the tide drops, packed with worms, clams and snails. It is a dinner table for shorebirds.
items.fun_fact: A single square yard of good mudflat can hold thousands of small animals.

items.name: King Tide
items.description: The highest tides of the year, when the sun and moon line up close to Earth in winter. Water reaches far up beaches and into the marsh.
items.fun_fact: Scientists photograph king tides to preview where everyday sea levels may reach in the future.

items.name: Ballona Creek
items.description: A long, mostly concrete-lined channel that drains much of LA's westside into the bay at Playa del Rey. Near the mouth, the tide still pushes in.
items.fun_fact: On a rising tide, salt water flows backward up the creek past the bike path.

items.name: Tide-Tuned Reeds
items.description: An invented reed that whistles the PointCast station chime when the evening breeze crosses the marsh. Birders say it is how the herons know it is time to fish.
items.fun_fact: Invented: each hollow stalk is said to be cut to a different note by the tide.

items.name: Mudlight Algae
items.description: An invented glowing algae that traces the tide line across the mudflats at night. From the air it draws the shape of the marsh in teal light.
items.fun_fact: Invented: the Gull's pilots use it as a landing light when the marine layer is thick.

items.name: Santa Ana Winds
items.description: Hot, dry winds that pour down from the deserts toward the coast, mostly in fall and winter. They bring crystal-clear views and high fire danger.
items.fun_fact: Offshore Santa Anas hold up the face of each wave and blow spray backward off the crest, a surfer's favorite sight.

items.name: Coastal Prickly Pear
items.description: A sprawling cactus with flat green pads and yellow flowers that grows on dry coastal slopes. Its purple fruit feeds birds and coyotes.
items.fun_fact: Cactus wrens and other animals use prickly pear thickets as safe hideouts from predators.

items.name: Lemonade Berry
items.description: A tough evergreen shrub with leathery leaves and clusters of sticky, reddish berries. It hugs the bluff tops above the sea.
items.fun_fact: Its berries are coated in a tart resin that people have soaked in water for a lemonade-like drink.

items.name: Toyon
items.description: A big native shrub with white summer flowers and bright red winter berries. Birds strip it clean by January.
items.fun_fact: It is often called California holly, and Hollywood is popularly said to be named after it.

items.name: Palos Verdes Blue Butterfly
items.description: A rare small blue butterfly found only on the Palos Verdes Peninsula. It feeds as a caterpillar on locoweed and deerweed.
items.fun_fact: It was thought extinct in the 1980s until a small population was rediscovered in 1994.

items.name: Bush Sunflower
items.description: A rounded shrub covered in yellow daisy flowers with dark centers. It brightens the bluffs after winter rains.
items.fun_fact: In summer drought it drops many leaves to save water, then leafs out again with the rains.

items.name: Catalina on the Horizon
items.description: On clear days Santa Catalina Island floats on the horizon about 20 miles off the peninsula. After a Santa Ana it looks close enough to swim to.
items.fun_fact: Locals read Catalina like a weather station: if you can see it sharply, the air is dry and clean.

items.name: Green Flash
items.description: A brief green spark at the top of the sun just as it sinks below a clear ocean horizon. The bluffs are one of the best places to try to see it.
items.fun_fact: It is caused by the atmosphere bending green light more than red, like a giant prism.

items.name: Portuguese Bend Landslide
items.description: A huge slow-moving landslide on the south side of the peninsula. Roads there are patched constantly as the land creeps toward the sea.
items.fun_fact: It is one of the most active landslides in the United States; the ground has been moving for decades.

items.name: Cliff Aster
items.description: A wiry native plant with white to pale pink dandelion-like flowers that clings to cliff faces. It blooms over a long season.
items.fun_fact: It roots in cracks where you would swear no soil exists.

items.name: Updraft Thistle
items.description: An invented thistle whose parachute seeds ride the cliff updrafts for miles. Glider pilots follow the seed clouds to find lift.
items.fun_fact: Invented: Aero Works test pilots call a good updraft day a thistle day.

items.name: Fog-Signal Lichen
items.description: An invented orange crust lichen on the bluff rocks that pulses gently whenever the lighthouse sweeps past. Sailors used to say it echoed the beam.
items.fun_fact: Invented, though real orange lichens do paint California sea cliffs in bright crusts.

items.name: Coral Tree
items.description: A wide, spreading tree that bursts into red-orange claw-shaped flowers in late winter. Many line boulevards across the Westside.
items.fun_fact: It is the official tree of the City of Los Angeles.

items.name: Jacaranda
items.description: A street tree that turns violet-blue with trumpet flowers in late spring. Fallen blossoms carpet sidewalks and parked cars.
items.fun_fact: Locals measure late spring by when the jacaranda purple shows up.

items.name: Mexican Fan Palm
items.description: The tall, skinny palm with a little round head that defines the Southern California skyline. Many were planted a century ago.
items.fun_fact: Some reach over 80 feet tall, wobbling in the wind like giant dandelions.

items.name: Bougainvillea
items.description: A thorny vine that pours over walls and garages in magenta, orange and red. It thrives in sun and neglect.
items.fun_fact: The bright color comes from papery bracts; the true flowers are the tiny white ones in the middle.

items.name: Bird of Paradise
items.description: An orange and blue flower shaped like a crested bird's head, rising on stiff stalks. It grows in nearly every South Bay garden.
items.fun_fact: It is the official flower of the City of Los Angeles.

items.name: Backyard Meyer Lemon
items.description: The lemon tree in the back corner of half the yards in town, heavy with fruit most of the year. Neighbors trade bags of them over the fence.
items.fun_fact: Meyer lemons are thought to be a cross between a lemon and a mandarin, which is why they taste sweeter.

items.name: California Sycamore
items.description: A big native shade tree with patchy, peeling white-and-tan bark and broad maple-like leaves. It shades parks and old streets.
items.fun_fact: Its bark peels off in jigsaw pieces as the trunk grows, so no two trunks look alike.

items.name: Nasturtium
items.description: A sprawling garden plant with round lily-pad leaves and orange and yellow flowers. It spills out of yards and vacant lots all over town.
items.fun_fact: Both the flowers and leaves are edible and taste peppery, like watercress.

items.name: Moreton Bay Fig
items.description: A giant fig with a broad canopy and huge roots that ripple across the ground. Old ones are local landmarks.
items.fun_fact: Its buttress roots can spread wider than the tree is tall.

items.name: Front-Yard Aloe
items.description: A spiky, branching succulent that blooms with orange-red torches in winter. It needs almost no water.
items.fun_fact: Its winter flowers are a key fuel stop for hummingbirds when little else is blooming.

items.name: Transistor Tulips
items.description: An invented garden bulb with cup-shaped petals that swivel toward the strongest broadcast. Front yards bloom in neat rows all facing the Lantern.
items.fun_fact: Invented: during the blackout, every tulip in town drooped at once.

items.name: Streamline Topiary
items.description: An invented hedge that grows on its own into jet-age shapes: fins, swoops and rocket noses. Gardeners only have to keep it watered.
items.fun_fact: Invented: the Aero Works lobby keeps one trimmed like the Gull.

items.name: Newsprint Ivy
items.description: An invented ivy whose cream leaves show faint gray patterns each morning, as if the weather report were printed on them. It climbs porch rails all along Main Street.
items.fun_fact: Invented: superstitious readers say a blank leaf means a slow news day.

items.name: The Moon
items.description: Earth's companion, whose pull raises and lowers the tides twice a day. Over the bay, a rising full moon lays a silver road across the water.
items.fun_fact: In Issue 1, the Lantern's knocked-off dish was beaming at the moon instead of El Segundo.

items.name: Evening Star
items.description: Venus, the brightest planet, often shines low in the west right after sunset or in the east before dawn. It is the first light many people see each evening.
items.fun_fact: Venus is so bright that it can cast faint shadows on a dark night far from city lights.

items.name: Orion
items.description: The great winter constellation, with three bright stars in a row for its belt. It rises over the South Bay on winter evenings.
items.fun_fact: Below the belt hangs the Orion Nebula, a star nursery you can see as a fuzzy spot with binoculars.

items.name: Perseid Meteor Shower
items.description: Each August, Earth passes through dust left by Comet Swift-Tuttle and meteors streak across the sky. The best hours are after midnight.
items.fun_fact: Perseid meteors hit the upper atmosphere at about 37 miles per second.

items.name: Lantern-Belt Micrometeors
items.description: An invented band of glittering dust that the Lantern's orbit crosses a few nights a year. A heavy shower of it knocked the dish off its mark in Issue 1.
items.fun_fact: Invented for the comic, but the station's dish shields were rebuilt after Issue 1.

items.name: Rocket Twilight Plume
items.description: When a rocket launches from the Central Coast just after sunset or before sunrise, its exhaust plume can glow in sunlight high above the dark ground. People across Southern California see a glowing jellyfish shape.
items.fun_fact: The plume shines because it is so high that it is still in sunlight while the ground below is dark.

items.name: Satellite Pass
items.description: A steady point of light gliding silently across the sky a little after dusk or before dawn. Unlike a plane, it does not blink.
items.fun_fact: Satellites are visible because they catch sunlight high above while the ground is already in shadow.

items.name: Milky Way
items.description: Our home galaxy, seen edge-on as a faint river of stars. City light hides it from town, but a dark trip south reveals it.
items.fun_fact: Every star you can see without a telescope is part of the Milky Way.

items.name: Earthshine
items.description: A faint glow on the dark part of a crescent moon. It is sunlight bouncing off Earth, lighting the moon's night side.
items.fun_fact: Leonardo da Vinci was the first to explain earthshine correctly, about 500 years ago.

items.name: Moonbounce
items.description: Radio operators really do bounce signals off the moon and hear them return to Earth about two and a half seconds later. Ham radio fans call it EME, Earth-Moon-Earth.
items.fun_fact: It is a real hobby; in the comic, the Lantern accidentally did it all night.

items.name: The Lantern Beacon
items.description: The comic's floating broadcast station, seen from town as a steady orange star high over the bay. Its signal carries the morning edition at 6:45.
items.fun_fact: Invented: this is the heart of the ecosystem map; half the inventions in this guide tune to it.

items.name: Signal Aurora
items.description: An invented ribbon of teal light that appears overhead when the Lantern runs at full power on a dry night. It ripples like a curtain over the bay.
items.fun_fact: Invented: real auroras are very rare this far south, which is why the town thinks theirs is special.

items.name: Solar Kelp
items.description: An invented kelp with mirrored blades that track the sun and store its warmth. Its forests float just offshore, glinting like a field of tinfoil.
items.fun_fact: Invented: the town imagines one day plugging the pier lights into it.

items.name: Beacon Moss
items.description: An invented moss that glows soft orange on rocks and rooftops, brighter when the Lantern is on the air. It carpets the shady side of town.
items.fun_fact: Invented: the moss is the town's backup signal meter; when it dims, someone calls the station.

items.name: Contrail Clouds
items.description: An invented weather where jet contrails linger and curl into ribbons, loops and arrowheads above the Aero Works. On busy days the sky looks hand-lettered.
items.fun_fact: Invented, though real contrails do sometimes spread into lasting cirrus clouds.

items.name: Radar Dandelion
items.description: An invented dandelion whose seed heads are tiny dish antennas. Each puff of wind sends a small cloud of receivers drifting over town.
items.fun_fact: Invented: kids make a wish and blow, and it supposedly picks up a song.

items.name: Static Fern
items.description: An invented fern whose fronds uncurl only when a strong broadcast passes nearby. In the morning they snap open all at once.
items.fun_fact: Invented: a fully curled fern at breakfast means the paper is late.

items.name: Jet-Bloom Hibiscus
items.description: An invented hibiscus with swept-back petals like delta wings. It leans into the wind and flutters audibly on breezy days.
items.fun_fact: Invented: the Gull's wing shape supposedly came from sketching one.

items.name: Thermos Cactus
items.description: An invented barrel cactus with a chrome-like skin that keeps its stored water ice cold. Desert pilots once carried cuttings as canteens.
items.fun_fact: Invented: tap it and it rings like a bottle.

items.name: Orbit Orchid
items.description: An invented orchid that grows weightless aboard the Lantern, roots drifting in the air. It is the station's only houseplant.
items.fun_fact: Invented: Rusty Vance waters it with an eyedropper at the end of every shift.

items.name: Tidewatch Lily
items.description: An invented water lily that opens on the rising tide and closes on the falling one. It floats in harbor slips and lagoon corners.
items.fun_fact: Invented: harbor masters keep a pot of them by the window as a tide gauge.

items.name: Fog Harp
items.description: An invented tall reed whose fine strings comb water out of the marine layer. Dew drips down each harp to water the dunes.
items.fun_fact: Invented, but real fog nets do collect drinking water from coastal fog in dry places.

items.name: Rocket Pinecone
items.description: An invented pine whose cones pop open only in the heat of a launch, scattering seed along the runways. Groves grow wherever rockets fly.
items.fun_fact: Invented, inspired by real pines whose cones open only after the heat of a wildfire.

items.name: Morning-Edition Marigold
items.description: An invented marigold that opens exactly at 6:45 A.M., when the paper goes out. Window boxes along Main Street flash orange in unison.
items.fun_fact: Invented: the first one bloomed late on the morning of the blackout, by about two hours.
